userDecisions.question: Who registers and owns MoonAliza's GitHub App, and what are its name and Homepage URL? Only the owning account can create the app. The build needs the app's client ID and install URL (both public, neither a credential), and the day-one checks need the registered app.
options: Your personal GitHub account (StepenkoAnatoli) owns it. The name is 'MoonAliza', or the nearest available name of at most 34 characters. The Homepage URL is https://github.com/StepenkoAnatoli/MoonAliza. The settings are those in F-23, and no client secret is generated. You send back the client ID and the install URL copied from the app's public page (Edit, Public page, Install), run the day-one checks DO-1..DO-15 with a second GitHub account, and ask GitHub Support the U-16 questions.
A GitHub organization you create for MoonAliza owns it, with the same settings and the same follow-up.

Register later: merge the sign-in with empty constants. The dialog says sign-in is not configured in this build, the e2e journey B is a visible skip and a release gate, and the app is registered before the first release that carries the feature.
userDecisions.recommended: Your personal GitHub account (StepenkoAnatoli) owns it. The name is 'MoonAliza', or the nearest available name of at most 34 characters. The Homepage URL is https://github.com/StepenkoAnatoli/MoonAliza. The settings are those in F-23, and no client secret is generated. You send back the client ID and the install URL copied from the app's public page (Edit, Public page, Install), run the day-one checks DO-1..DO-15 with a second GitHub account, and ask GitHub Support the U-16 questions.
userDecisions.why: This is the quickest way to a working sign-in that is tested end to end before the merge. The repository already lives under that account, and only the owning account can register the app (E-03). The name must be unique and at most 34 characters (E-03 l.53), so whether 'MoonAliza' is free is known only at registration. The install URL is copied, never derived from the name (R2-8, E-12 l.49-53). Whoever owns the app, its per-app limits may apply across every install (U-16). The research does not cover moving an app to an organization later, so option 2 is the one to pick if organization ownership matters. Option 3 lets the code merge first, but nobody can use the feature until registration, and the full Windows journey cannot run before then.

userDecisions.question: Is the GitHub connection read-only for private repository reading now, or the single shared connection the plan describes for research collection, private reading and the later write steps (docs/superpowers/plans/2026-10-02-research-jobs.md:426, :491)?
options: Read-only now: Contents and Metadata read-only. The research collector keeps its pasted token, the plan's lines 426 and 491 get a correction note, and the write path is designed in its own task.
Register with the broader permissions now: Actions read and write for the collector's dispatch, and Contents and Pull requests write for self-unblocking, so one connection serves every later step.
Read-only now, and a second, separate GitHub App later for writes.
userDecisions.recommended: Read-only now: Contents and Metadata read-only. The research collector keeps its pasted token, the plan's lines 426 and 491 get a correction note, and the write path is designed in its own task.
userDecisions.why: Every read read_github makes needs only Contents read (E-05 l.1007-1036), and the plan's own step 1 asks for least privilege. The collector cannot share this token anyway: each refresh kills the old access token (E-02 l.36), a watch child holds its token for up to an hour (src/adapters/research-kit/collector.ts:50), and the collector needs Actions write. The cost is widening later: every installing owner must approve new permissions, and their installation keeps the old ones until they do (E-19 l.26-28, E-04 l.57). That is acceptable because no write feature exists yet. Option 3 keeps reading and writing permanently apart, at the cost of a second registration.

userDecisions.question: How is private repository text that the agent reads treated? Cloud-allowed conversations send it to the selected provider, and it is stored and full-text indexed with the conversation.
options: Like local project files. It is allowed in any conversation where the user pasted the URL. A local-only conversation sends it nowhere; a cloud-allowed one sends it to the selected provider. Tool results stay in the conversation's history and search. Sign-out does not delete them; deleting the conversation removes them from MoonAliza. The GitHub dialog, the composer note, one clause in the cloud dialog and the spec say so, and no text claims erasure.
Private reads only in local-only conversations: a cloud-allowed conversation is refused a private read.
As the first option, plus deleting stored private-repository tool results at sign-out.
userDecisions.recommended: Like local project files. It is allowed in any conversation where the user pasted the URL. A local-only conversation sends it nowhere; a cloud-allowed one sends it to the selected provider. Tool results stay in the conversation's history and search. Sign-out does not delete them; deleting the conversation removes them from MoonAliza. The GitHub dialog, the composer note, one clause in the cloud dialog and the spec say so, and no text claims erasure.
userDecisions.why: It reuses the existing, tested policy: main checks the conversation's inference policy before and after every read (src/main/index.ts:113-121, src/engine/policy.ts:68-78), and local project files already follow these rules. Options 2 and 3 both need MoonAliza to know which repositories are private, which means an extra GitHub call per repository and a new policy rule. Option 3 also deletes user data, which is on the stop-list. The bytes of deleted conversations may remain in SQLite free pages or the WAL (secure_delete is not set), so the wording never says erased; secure_delete is recorded for later.

userDecisions.question: When signed in, does read_github send the token on every read, or only when a repository is not readable without it?
options: Every read while signed in, with no unauthenticated fallback when the token cannot be used.
Unauthenticated first, repeated with the token only after a 404.
userDecisions.recommended: Every read while signed in, with no unauthenticated fallback when the token cannot be used.
userDecisions.why: It is one request per read and one behaviour. Signed-in reads use the user's own 5,000 requests an hour instead of the 60 an hour per IP that unauthenticated requests get (prior E-08 l.40, l.46, l.60). The cost: GitHub sees the user's identity on public reads too, and the 5,000 is shared with the user's other apps and tokens; the dialog discloses both. Option 2 keeps public reads anonymous, but doubles the requests for private repositories and spends the anonymous allowance on each one. A fallback after a token failure would turn a renewal problem into a misleading 'not found'.

userDecisions.question: Which network stack carries the sign-in, the refresh and signed-in reads? Reviewed decision 4 (docs/specification/decisions.md:8) asks for an Electron network broker with the system proxy, but every GitHub call today uses Node's global fetch.
options: Node's global fetch, late-bound in main for the sign-in and through the reader's per-run default for reads, as read_github and the verified import use today. The spec records that its Windows proxy and certificate behaviour is unverified and that this diverges from decision 4, and moving every GitHub call to the Electron broker together is recorded for later.
Electron's providers session (system proxy and certificate checks, per decision 4) for the sign-in, the refresh and signed-in reads, while signed-out reads stay on global fetch.
Move every GitHub call (reader, verified import, sign-in) to the Electron session now.
userDecisions.recommended: Node's global fetch, late-bound in main for the sign-in and through the reader's per-run default for reads, as read_github and the verified import use today. The spec records that its Windows proxy and certificate behaviour is unverified and that this diverges from decision 4, and moving every GitHub call to the Electron broker together is recorded for later.
userDecisions.why: Every existing GitHub call uses Node's fetch (src/main/github.ts:12, src/main/research-import.ts:69), and the GitHub e2e intercepts it there (e2e/github-reading.spec.ts:31-46). With one stack, sign-in cannot succeed on a network where reads then fail. Electron's session.fetch enforces redirect 'error' (docs/specification/more-models.md:123), so options 2 and 3 would change the reader's 3xx handling. They would also need a github.com TLS fake, which breaks a pinned test. The cost of option 1: a user whose network needs the Windows system proxy, or TLS inspection, may not reach GitHub, exactly as public reads today. Option 1 departs from a reviewed decision, which is why it is the user's call.

userDecisions.question: Conditional, decided only if day-one check DO-1 fails: if a token produced by a refresh cannot be refreshed again without a client secret, what does MoonAliza do?
options: Ask the user to sign in again with the device flow whenever the access token expires (about every 8 hours of use).
Turn off 'Expire user authorization tokens' in the registration, so tokens do not expire.
userDecisions.recommended: Ask the user to sign in again with the device flow whenever the access token expires (about every 8 hours of use).
userDecisions.why: Shipping a client secret is ruled out (F-20, F-27). GitHub strongly recommends keeping token expiry on (E-03). A non-expiring token stays valid until it is revoked, which is worse for privacy, and the one-year-unused revocation is stated only for OAuth apps (E-09). Signing in again costs a device flow each time, and each one may count against a per-app cap (U-16). That is acceptable for the current single user, and it is revisited if the user base grows. The build needs no change for option 1: a failed second refresh already clears the account and shows 'sign in again'.

userDecisions.question: Approve 1 Firecrawl credit to collect GitHub's own device-flow tutorial, 'Building a CLI with a GitHub App' (linked from E-01 l.112), so the parameter placement of the device-flow and refresh requests (URL query or form body) is settled before the wire client is briefed? The run's 20-credit budget is spent, and raising it is the operator's decision (Research-Kit Rule 5).
options: Approve 1 credit; the lead collects the page into the design project, adds an E-row, and briefs U1 with the confirmed placement.
Do not collect: U1 builds the form-body placement in one function, pinned by a test, and day-one check DO-2 confirms it with the registered app before release.
userDecisions.recommended: Approve 1 credit; the lead collects the page into the design project, adds an E-row, and briefs U1 with the confirmed placement.
userDecisions.why: The pages call the inputs 'query parameters' but use the same words for response fields (E-01 l.118, l.122, l.138, l.167), so the placement is not stated. A refresh token or device code in a URL is visible to anything that records URLs, and a body is not, which is why the design chose the body (DR-9). The design has no runtime fallback between placements, because a refresh token is single-use (E-02 l.36). If the guess is wrong, every sign-in fails in the field until one function changes. One credit settles it before any code depends on it; without it, the risk waits for the day-one check.

dayOneChecks: DO-1 (U-4, verifier F-4): with the registered app, run the device flow, then refresh twice in a row with no client secret; both must succeed. E-02 l.79 exempts only tokens generated using the device flow, and is worded per token. Until checked, the build refreshes without a secret. If a refresh fails, its error clears the account and the user is asked to sign in again (bad_refresh_token, or an unknown error that holds for 30 s). Staying signed in for six months is labelled as resting on this check, and a failure goes to UD-6 before release.

DO-2 (OF-1), only if the OF-1 credit is not approved: confirm that github.com/login/device/code and github.com/login/oauth/access_token accept their parameters in a form-encoded body, for step 1, the poll and the refresh. Until then, the build sends them in the body, with no query string, from one function (oauthRequest) pinned by a test. It never falls back to the query form, because a refresh token is single-use (E-02 l.36).

DO-3 (prior E-01 l.200-221): record the Content-Type and body shape of a device-code answer and a token answer sent with Accept: application/json. Until then, the build parses JSON and form-encoded bodies by Content-Type, comparing case-insensitively before ';', and treats any other type as unparseable (transient).

DO-4 (R2-3, V3-4, U-2): sign in first, then install the app on the user's own account with Only select repositories. Read a selected private repository with the existing token, then add another repository to the installation and read it. Repeat on an organization installation, and with a repository added by a repository admin, if one is available; otherwise record that the own-account result is assumed to carry over. Record whether each read works without a new sign-in, and how soon. Until then, every install or add route in the signed-in 404 text ends with 'if it still fails after the app is installed or given the repository, the user signs in to MoonAliza again'. That line is removed if reads work at once.

DO-5 (U-5): send a request with an access token past its expiry, and record the status (401, or 404 on a private repository). Until then, the build never knowingly sends an expired token: it refreshes when under 300 s are left, and refreshes first after a clock step back of more than 300 s. A 401 goes through the 401 rule. A 404 shows the signed-in 404 text, which ends with 'sign in again'.

DO-6 (U-4, R2-5): refresh once with an already-used refresh token, and record the status and body of bad_refresh_token. Until then, the build reads 'error' from the body at any HTTP status, after classifying rate limits first, and bad_refresh_token clears the account whatever the status.

DO-7 (U-10, R2-2): read a private repository in three situations: on the user's own account before installing; in an organization where the user is a member but not an owner; and in a SAML organization without an active session. Record each status and its headers. In the SAML case, then start a SAML session and retry with the same token, recording whether it reaches the organization without a new sign-in. Until then, the 404 and 403 texts list the possibilities and claim none, and the SAML remedy has both steps: start a SAML session for the organization on GitHub, then sign in to MoonAliza again.

DO-8 (R2-4): observe how github.com/login/oauth/access_token and /login/device/code answer when rate-limited (statuses, x-ratelimit-* headers, retry-after, body), from GitHub Support or a test account. Until then, the build applies E-15's REST rules as a precaution, classified before any error or success: a 429, a 403 with remaining 0, or a 403/429 with retry-after. It waits retry-after, else the reset (at least 60 s, at most 1 h), else 60 s. A refresh is held until the wait passes, and a poll whose wait would pass the deadline ends as rate-limited.

DO-9 (U-16, KNOWN-UNKNOWN): ask GitHub Support three questions. Does the device flow's 50-submissions-per-hour cap (stated for OAuth apps, prior E-01 l.307) apply to GitHub Apps, and is it counted per app? Is the 2,000 OAuth access token requests per hour (prior E-08 l.95) counted per app or per user? Do polls and refreshes count toward it? Record the answers in DISCOVERY.md. Until then, the build assumes per-app counting: user-initiated starts only, one flow at a time, closing the dialog cancels, interval and slow_down honoured, rate limits classified first, and holds after failed refreshes. The 'expired' outcome text says GitHub may be limiting sign-ins. The spec records the arithmetic as a product risk: about 180 polls per sign-in left pending, and refreshes at about active users x 3 / 24 an hour, reaching 2,000 an hour at about 16,000 users active across a day.

DO-10 (U-15): call GET https://api.github.com/user with the app's user token, and confirm the response carries 'login'. Until then, the login is read once, after storing (one-shot, outside the 401 rule). Any failure leaves login null, the sign-in stays, and the dialog shows 'Signed in to GitHub (account name unavailable)'.

DO-11 (U-8, U-11): after registering with Any account, confirm that the app's public page shows an Install button to a second GitHub account. Until then, that Any account means public is recorded as an inference (E-14 l.20, E-03 l.93).

DO-12 (E-01 l.128-132): record a live device-code answer: whether verification_uri equals https://github.com/login/device exactly, the user_code shape (8 characters with a hyphen), device_code length, expires_in, interval, and the app name and permissions GitHub's device page shows the user. Until then, the build accepts only the exact verification_uri (any other value ends the attempt as start-failed, fail closed). It accepts user codes matching alphanumeric groups joined by hyphens, at most 32 characters, and any printable device_code up to 1,024 characters. The phishing text asks the user to check that they are authorizing MoonAliza's GitHub App.

DO-13 (R2-1, E-15 l.108): provoke a real permission 403 on a signed-in read (for example, an installation whose owner has not approved an updated permission, if available), and record whether the body contains 'Resource not accessible by integration' and whether X-Accepted-GitHub-Permissions accompanies it. Until then, a signed-in 403 with that body text is GITHUB_PERMISSION_MISSING. Any other signed-in 403 is GITHUB_FORBIDDEN_SIGNED_IN, whose text still leads with the permission cause. The header is never the test.

DO-14 (R2-8, E-12 l.49-53): open the install URL copied from the app's public page, from the built app's Install on repositories button, and confirm that GitHub shows the app's installation page. Until then, the constant is empty and the dialog says sign-in is not configured. The constants test requires the shape https://github.com/apps/<name>/installations/new.

DO-15 (E-10 l.145, U-6): confirm that a real sign-in's access and refresh tokens pass the shape check (ghu_ and ghr_ prefixes, header-safe characters, at most 16,384 characters), and that a refresh answer has the same shape, without recording any token value. Until then, the check assumes only the prefix and what a header can carry. A failed check stores nothing: a sign-in ends failed, and a 2xx refresh with a malformed access_token clears the account (fail closed).

findings.evidence:
- Spec 2.1, row A4: 'a transient failure, an unknown `error`, an unusable answer, or the capability denied twice -> A3, held | hold for 30 s; waiters get GITHUB_RENEWAL_UNAVAILABLE'.
- DR-4: 'A transient failure, an unknown `error` or an unusable answer keeps the vault ... and holds for 30 s'.
- L-12 lists only `bad_refresh_token` among `error` codes that clear the account.
- E-01 capture l.256: 'If the `client_id` or `client_secret` that you specify are incorrect, you will receive an `incorrect_client_credentials` error.'
- E-02 l.79: the secret exemption is worded per token. DR-1 Risks: 'If the second refresh without a secret fails (DO-1), users sign in every 8 hours'.
- The outcome table maps `incorrect_client_credentials` to `client-rejected` for flows only, not for refresh.
- The 3.9 reason table gives GITHUB_RENEWAL_UNAVAILABLE retry `same-request`.
findings.fix:
Classify refresh `error` codes explicitly:
- `bad_refresh_token`, `incorrect_client_credentials` and `unsupported_grant_type`: clear the account (A2, sign-in required) at any status. For `incorrect_client_credentials`, also set an in-memory ended reason so the dialog can say that GitHub rejected MoonAliza's registration.
- An unknown code: hold with doubling (30 s, 60 s, ... capped at 1 h). Clear after 3 consecutive identical `error` answers.

Add these to L-12 and DR-4.

Tests, each at status 200 and at a 4xx:
- a refresh answering `incorrect_client_credentials` ends the account after exactly 1 refresh request, and the next read throws GITHUB_SIGN_IN_REQUIRED;
- an unknown code three times ends the account after at most 3 refresh requests, with the gaps between them growing.

Record in DO-1 what the second refresh actually returns.

findings.problem: The design clears the account on a 401 for a token that a refresh has just issued. Three rules do this: C-6 (a 401 on the token this call's own refresh produced), F-8 (the retried call still gets 401), and the 'rotated meanwhile, retry with the current token' path. All three assume a newly issued user token is accepted by api.github.com at once. The corpus does not say so, and no day-one check tests it: DO-1 runs two refreshes but never uses the new token straight away. If GitHub propagates new tokens with a delay, or answers 401 during an incident, a routine refresh followed by its immediate retry wipes a pair that is valid and was just rotated. The user is then signed out, about every 8 hours under load, and must run the device flow again, spending per-app quota (U-16).
findings.evidence:
- REQUIREMENTS F-8 (Stage 3, C-6): 'a 401 on the token it produced clears the account'. Spec 2.1, row A3: 'a 401 under the 401 rule -> A2 clearIf(accessRef)'. F-8: 'The account is cleared only when the refresh returns bad_refresh_token or the retried call still gets 401.'
- The retry is sent in the same call, milliseconds after the new pair is committed (L-4, 3.4).
- E-01 l.44 gives 401 for revoked tokens only. No capture says when a refreshed token becomes valid.
- A lead only, not corpus evidence: GitHub's own SDK, @octokit/auth-app, retries 401s on installation tokens younger than 5 s 'to account for token replication delay'. That is a sibling token type, not a statement about user tokens.
findings.fix:
Add a day-one check, DO-16: refresh, then at once send GET /user and a private read with the new token. Repeat 20 times and record each status and its delay.

Until DO-16 passes, add an age guard in code:
- A 401 on a token whose receivedAt is under 5 s ago waits 1 s, then 2 s, and retries the same token. The waits stay within the read's deadline and are not a refresh, so the C-6 budget is unchanged.
- If the token is still under 5 s old when the budget runs out, fail the call as GITHUB_RENEWAL_UNAVAILABLE and keep the account. Only a 401 on a token older than 5 s takes the clear path.

Tests: the fake answers 401 twice, then 200, for a token 0-2 s old: the account is kept and the call succeeds. A token older than 5 s that gets 401 after its refresh is cleared.

findings.problem: The UD-6 fallback ('the owner turns expiry off') does nothing while the build sends `scope=offline_access` at step 1. GitHub documents that this scope forces expiring tokens with a refresh token even when the app has expiry disabled. So if DO-1 fails, deselecting 'Expire user authorization tokens' in the registration still yields 8-hour tokens that need the refresh that does not work. The fallback silently needs a code change that the design does not mention.
findings.evidence:
- Spec 5.1, step 1 parameters: `client_id`, `scope=offline_access`. DR-1: 'Sign-in. The device flow with scope=offline_access.'
- E-01 capture l.120: 'To get to an expiring user access token and a refresh token for this authorization even if your app has them disabled, you can also send the `scope` query parameter with the value `offline_access`.'
- E-02 l.40: '... even if your app is configured not to use expiring tokens'. E-02 l.42: 'The only supported value is `offline_access`, which forces the user access token to expire.'
- DR-1 Risks: '... users sign in every 8 hours, or the owner turns expiry off (UD-6)'.
findings.fix: Record in DR-1, DO-1 and UD-6 that the expiry-off fallback also needs step 1 to drop `scope=offline_access`. Make the scope a frozen main-only constant in `src/main/github-app.ts` (for example `REQUEST_OFFLINE_ACCESS = true`) that is flipped together with the registration. Add a wire test that pins the parameter and a constants test that pins the pairing. State that accounts already signed in keep their expiring pair until they sign in again.

findings.problem:
The admit rule for a sign-in's commit is not defined, and both natural readings are wrong.
- **If the commit is admitted against the generation (L-6):** a 'Sign in again' is refused whenever the old account's generation changes during the flow, which can last up to 15 minutes. That happens when the old account refreshes (A4 -> A3, generation++) or is cleared by the app (bad_refresh_token or the 401 rule). The second case is common: the user revoked on GitHub, reads start failing, and they choose Sign in again. The user authorized on github.com and gets `failed`.
- **If the commit is admitted only while 'the flow is current':** F4 is 'not interruptible', so a sign-out during F4 does not stop it. replace() step 6 sets live = next after clear()'s synchronous prologue has already set live = null. clear's locked part then removes the refs the file names, which are the new ones. live now points at removed refs, and the dialog shows signed-in.
findings.evidence:
- L-6: 'Every account mutation ... is admitted against the generation it was based on.'
- 2.1: row 'A4 | the refresh succeeds ... | A3 (new pair) | generation++'; row 'A1..A4 | a flow reaches its commit point | A3 (new) | ... the result of an A4 refresh is discarded', which implies the sign-in always wins over a refresh.
- 2.2, F4: 'Not interruptible; a Cancel from here on is a no-op'. F-11: sign-out 'cancels a pending flow'.
- 4.3, step 6: 'if it fails, return null. A clear has begun.' 4.3 clear(): the prologue sets live = null; the locked part 'removes every ref the file names'.
- The supplied spec text ends in 6.1, so 6.3 may define the rule. Nothing in the text reviewed does.

findings.problem:
The spec contradicts itself about Cancel after the commit point.
- F4 and F-10 say Cancel is a no-op from the commit point on.
- The signal table says Cancel aborts F5's GET /user, and the login then 'stays unknown'.
- F4 and F5 project as `pending` (2.3 rule 2), so the renderer cannot tell F2 from F5. Closing the dialog therefore cancels (D-5).

A user who approves on github.com and then closes the dialog during F4/F5 (up to 20 s) is left with `login: null` for good. L-2 allows GET /user only right after a commit, so only another sign-in recovers the login, and that spends a device code (U-16). If cancel() also records `cancelled`, the status shows signed-in with lastOutcome 'cancelled'. The pending text 'closing the dialog cancels' is false once the commit point has passed.
findings.evidence:
- 2.2, F4: 'a Cancel from here on is a no-op'. F-10: 'After the commit point, Cancel is a no-op.'
- 2.5, row 'GET /user (F5)': aborted by 'Cancel, sign-out, quit (the login stays unknown)'.
- 2.3 rule 2: 'F4 and F5 stay pending'. F-10/D-5: 'Closing the GitHub dialog cancels a pending flow'. F-1: the pending view says 'closing the dialog cancels'.
- L-2: GitHub traffic only from start(), polls, 'the GET /user after a commit point', and send().
findings.fix:
Make cancel() a true no-op from F4 on: no abort of F5 and no outcome recorded. Only signOut() and quit abort F5. Add `committed: boolean` to the pending DTO, or project F4/F5 as signed-in with `login: null`, so that:
- the dialog stops saying 'closing cancels' after the commit;
- closing does not call cancel at that point.

Test: cancel and dialog close during a slow F5 leave the login set when GET /user answers, with lastOutcome null.

findings.problem:
Sign-out says it 'swallows disk errors because startup finishes the job'. Startup can only finish the job if either the vault's tombstone or the account-file write reached disk. If both fail, the sign-out is undone at the next start, and the user's tokens, still valid on GitHub, come back:
- Both writes go to the same volume through temp-file-plus-rename, so disk-full or a Windows rename lock can fail both.
- At the next start, account.json is still valid and names the refs, and index.json still says committed.
- So open() and finishStartup see committed refs and return A3: signed in again.

Meanwhile the method returned success, and the F-12 text told the user 'MoonAliza deleted its copy on this computer'.
findings.evidence:
- Spec 3.3: 'github.signOut | local only (6.7); disk errors are swallowed, because startup finishes the job'. 4.3 clear(): 'Disk errors are swallowed, because startup completes the job.'
- `src/main/vault.ts:164-170`: tombstone() changes only the in-memory index synchronously. Durability comes from `persist()` (:71-79, temp file then rename), whose failure the design swallows.
- `src/models/artifact-files.ts:49-56`: atomicJson also uses temp file then rename.
- Spec 2.1 startup row: 'a valid file whose refs are committed (vault.has) ... -> A3'. `vault.has` reads the on-disk state after restart (`src/main/vault.ts:123-127`).
- F-12 (1): 'MoonAliza deleted its copy on this computer'.
findings.fix:
Have signOut() await and observe the tombstone persist and the account-file write.
- If at least one is durable, keep today's behaviour.
- If neither is durable, retry once. If that fails too, return `signed-out` with a non-secret flag such as `signOutIncomplete: true`. The dialog then shows 'MoonAliza could not finish removing its copy; it will retry when MoonAliza restarts' instead of the deletion claim. Keep the in-memory tombstone so the next successful vault persist records it.

Test: a vault stub whose persist rejects plus a file write that fails, then reopen the store with the vault's on-disk index. Today's design reads signed-in, so the test should be red until the fix.

findings.problem:
Guard G-19 says every 'GITHUB_[A-Z_]+' literal in `src/main/github*.ts` must parse in GitHubErrorCodeSchema. It conflicts with another unit's frozen API, and it cannot be proved in the unit that owns it:
- `src/main/github-account-store.ts` (U2) matches the glob and contains the literal 'GITHUB_STORE_FAILED' (ReplaceFailure), which is not a reader reason. G-19 is therefore certain to go red when U2 and U3 are integrated.
- U3 writes the guard in wave 1, when U5's `github-signin.ts` does not exist yet. U5 is the only place GITHUB_SIGN_IN_REQUIRED and GITHUB_RENEWAL_UNAVAILABLE are thrown. Removing those members from the enum leaves G-19 green in U3's worktree, so its removal proof cannot be done there.
findings.evidence:
- Spec 3.6: `class ReplaceFailure extends Error { constructor(readonly written: boolean) { super('GITHUB_STORE_FAILED'); } }`.
- Spec 3.9: 'A guard test pins both: every 'GITHUB_[A-Z_]+' literal in src/main/github*.ts must parse in the enum.'
- BREAKDOWN: U3 is in wave 1 and its pre-mortem (2) names G-19; U2 is in wave 1; U5 is in wave 2.
- The rules for every unit say 'Every guard has a removal proof'.
- `src/main/engine.ts:60-61` collapses unknown codes to GITHUB_UNAVAILABLE.
findings.fix:
Change the frozen contract in two ways:
- Rename ReplaceFailure's message to a non-GITHUB_ code, for example 'ACCOUNT_STORE_FAILED'.
- Freeze in U0 an exported tuple `CREDENTIAL_ERRORS = ['GITHUB_SIGN_IN_REQUIRED', 'GITHUB_RENEWAL_UNAVAILABLE', 'GITHUB_RATE_LIMIT'] as const` in `src/main/github-credential.ts`. U5 throws only members of it.

G-19 then asserts that every member of CREDENTIAL_ERRORS and every reader reason parses in the enum, which can be proved red in U3. Keep the source-literal scan as an integration test owned by U6, scoped to `throw new Error('...')` sites.

findings.problem: The design adds 'github' to `src/shared/host.ts` PurposeSchema, exports it, and adds a test that keeps it equal to the vault's union. But that schema is the `purpose` of HostMessageSchema's engine-side `network.request` payload, which is bound to a profile. Adding 'github' says the engine may name a GitHub-credential purpose. That contradicts 'Engine protocol: 0 new messages' and F-22 ('The engine gets no sign-in message'). The equality test would also force every future main-only vault purpose into the engine-facing schema. No production code needs it.
findings.evidence:
- `src/shared/host.ts:4`: `const PurposeSchema = z.enum([...])` (not exported) feeds `binding.purpose` in HostMessageSchema (:5-9) and `authorizeHostMessage` (:12-19). It is used only by tests/contracts.test.ts:151-163 and re-exported to every bundle through src/shared/index.ts:6.
- Spec 3.8 and BREAKDOWN U0: 'PurposeSchema ... gains 'github'. A typecheck-level test keeps it equal to the vault union.'
- Spec 1: 'Engine protocol | 0 new messages'.
findings.fix: Leave `src/shared/host.ts` unchanged and drop it from U0's owned files. If a guard is wanted, assert that host purposes are a subset of vault purposes and that 'github' is not among the host purposes (typecheck-level), so the engine can never name it.

findings.evidence:
- Spec 2.4 L-7: 'A token exists in clear only in two places ... No token is ever held in a field, a closure that outlives the request, an error or its cause ...'. 2.4 heading: '(each is a named test)'.
- Spec 3.5: `requestToken(fetcher, params, ...)` takes the refresh token inside `params`.
- `src/main/github.ts:15-16`: the init object is built inline. `src/main/github.ts:81` wraps errors with `{ cause: error }`.

findings.problem:
The file schema caps `retiredRefs` at 8, but the writer can exceed the cap:
- replace() step 4 writes `[current refs (up to 2) + existing retiredRefs]`;
- step 7 clears the list, but its write failures are swallowed.

After four rotations whose step-7 writes failed, all in one session, the file has 10 retired refs. Its own reader then rejects it (the 8 cap), and open() reads it as 'no account'. The user is signed out, and the live committed refs become orphans the reconcile never deletes. clear() likewise writes `account refs + retiredRefs`, which can be up to 10.
findings.evidence:
- Spec 4.2: `retiredRefs: z.array(SecretRef).max(8)`.
- Spec 4.3, step 4: `retiredRefs: [the refs the file names now, plus its retiredRefs]`. Step 7: 'Failures here are swallowed'.
- 4.4: 'A missing, invalid ... file reads as no account'.
- `src/main/vault.ts:106-121`: the reconcile never deletes committed entries.
findings.fix: Before step 4 writes, if the list would exceed 8, retire the oldest entries first (tombstone, remove, tolerating CREDENTIAL_NOT_TOMBSTONED) and keep at most 8. Alternatively, raise the bound to cover the worst case and refuse the replace beyond it. Test: four replaces with the step-7 write failing, then reopen: the account still reads, and the file passes AccountFileSchema.

findings.problem:
F-10 says a failed 'Sign in again' leaves the existing account untouched. But when ReplaceFailure(true) is thrown during a sign-in (the file is written and the commit fails), step 4 has already moved the existing account's refs into `retiredRefs` and named the new staged refs as the account. The session keeps the old account. The next start then:
- tombstones the old account's refs (open() retires `retiredRefs`);
- commits the 'failed' new pair, because the reconcile commits referenced staged refs.

The user, who was told the sign-in failed, comes back signed in as the new and possibly different GitHub user.
findings.evidence:
- Spec 4.3, steps 4 and 5: 'This write is the crash-recovery commit point' and 'On failure, throw ReplaceFailure(true)'.
- 4.4 step 1: open() 'tombstones retiredRefs'.
- 4.5: 'the file write, before commit -> ... the reconcile commits them; signed in with the new pair'.
- F-10: 'If the new flow is cancelled or fails, the existing account is left untouched.'
- The outcome table maps 'storing failed' to `failed`.
findings.fix: For a sign-in, handle ReplaceFailure(true) by rewriting the file back to the previous account and its retiredRefs, then tombstoning and removing the staged pair; report `failed` only if that rollback succeeds. If the rollback fails, treat the commit point as reached: report the sign-in as stored, and let startup's reconcile finish. Test: during 'Sign in again', commit throws; reopen and reconcile; the documented account results.

findings.problem: rateLimitWait has no lower bound. `retry-after: 0` produces a 0 ms hold, so after a rate-limited refresh L-13 gives no protection. Every read can send another refresh to the shared endpoint, and each fails as GITHUB_RATE_LIMIT.
findings.evidence:
- Spec 5.4: '1. retry-after, if it is an integer from 0 to 3,600: that many seconds ... The result is clamped to at most rateLimitCeilingMs.' The 60 s floor applies only to rules 2 and 3.
- 2.1, row 'A4 | the refresh is rate-limited | A3, held | hold until the wait passes'.
- L-13: 'No refresh request is sent while a hold is active.'
findings.fix: Clamp the result to at least 1 s for polls (which also keep their `interval` floor), and to at least `transientHoldMs` for refresh holds. Test: a 429 with retry-after 0 on a refresh, followed by two reads: one refresh request in total.

findings.problem: L-10's pin compares the signed-out init by deep equality. Two AbortSignal objects compare equal under vitest's toEqual, because neither has own enumerable keys. So the pin cannot detect a mutation that drops Stop or the 20 s timeout from `init.signal`. No existing test checks that Stop reaches the fetcher's signal: the existing Stop test checks only the post-response abort check.
findings.evidence:
- Spec L-10: 'the same URL and the same init object it builds today'. BREAKDOWN U3, commit 1: 'the signed-out init deep-equal pin'.
- `src/main/github.ts:15` passes `signal` (`AbortSignal.any([stop, timeout])`, :38).
- `tests/github-read.test.ts:58-60` ('Stop discards a late response even when transport ignores abort') never inspects `init.signal`.

findings.problem: The vault cap test, 'a github grant over 30 s denied and one at 30 s allowed', is flaky if 'over' means a 1 ms margin. grant() reads Date.now() again (`binding.expiresAt > Date.now() + 30_000`), so a test passing `Date.now() + 30_001` is denied only when no millisecond passes between the two reads.
findings.evidence:
- `src/main/vault.ts:135`. BREAKDOWN U0 tests: 'a github grant over 30 s denied and one at 30 s allowed'.
- The existing research cap test uses a 60 s margin (`tests/vault.test.ts:41`).
findings.fix: Use `Date.now() + 60_000` for the denied case, as tests/vault.test.ts:41 does, or stub Date.now; keep `Date.now() + 30_000` for the allowed case. Check the removal proof, 'red when :135 is left alone', with the 60 s case.

findings.problem: The client-ID mismatch case at startup is classified two ways. The 2.1 startup row sends it to A1 (`ended: false`). But L-12 lists 'open() finding another non-empty client ID' among the app's own clears, and A2 is defined as 'the app cleared it (the L-12 cases)'. Under A1, a user whose sign-in was dropped by a re-registration sees a plain 'signed out' with no explanation.
findings.evidence:
- Spec 2.1 startup row: '... or it names another non-empty client ID | A1'.
- 2.1 A2: 'No account, because the app cleared it (the L-12 cases) | signed-out, ended: true'.
- L-12, last bullet: '`open()` finding another non-empty client ID'.
findings.fix: Pick one. Recommended: A2. open() sets an in-memory ended flag that the projection reads, so `ended` is true. Add a store or service test: a file with another client ID gives status `signed-out` with `ended: true` and zero fetcher calls.
